## Proof

Let $\mathbb{N} = \{0,1,2,\dots\}$. A relation $R$ on $\mathbb{N}$ is a subset of $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$, so the set of all relations is $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N})$, which has cardinality $2^{|\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}|} = 2^{\aleph_0}$.

We want the cardinality of
$$X = \{R \subseteq \mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N} : R^{*} = \mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}\}.$$

**Upper bound.** Since $X \subseteq \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N})$, we have $|X| \le 2^{\aleph_0}$.

**Lower bound.** We exhibit $2^{\aleph_0}$ distinct relations all having transitive closure $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$.

Define the "backbone" relation
$$R_0 = \{(n, n+1) : n \in \mathbb{N}\} \cup \{(n+1, n) : n \in \mathbb{N}\}.$$
This is the edge relation of the one-way infinite path made bidirectional between consecutive naturals. For any $a, b \in \mathbb{N}$:
- If $a < b$, there is a path $a \to a+1 \to \cdots \to b$ in $R_0$.
- If $a > b$, there is a path $a \to a-1 \to \cdots \to b$ in $R_0$.
- If $a = b$, there is a path $a \to a+1 \to a$ in $R_0$ (length 2), so $(a,a) \in R_0^{*}$ even under the non-reflexive definition of transitive closure; under the reflexive definition it is automatic.

Hence $R_0^{*} = \mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$.

Now for **every** subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$, define $R_S = R_0 \cup S$. Since $R_0 \subseteq R_S$, monotonicity of the transitive closure gives
$$\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N} = R_0^{*} \subseteq R_S^{*} \subseteq \mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N},$$
so $R_S^{*} = \mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$. Thus $R_S \in X$ for every $S$.

The map $S \mapsto R_S = R_0 \cup S$ is injective (distinct $S$ give distinct $R_S$, since they differ outside $R_0$ — indeed if $S_1 \ne S_2$, pick $(a,b)$ in the symmetric difference; then $(a,b) \in R_{S_1}\triangle R_{S_2}$, and note $(a,b) \in R_0$ would put it in both, contradiction, so it genuinely distinguishes). Therefore
$$|X| \ge |\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N})| = 2^{\aleph_0}.$$

**Conclusion.** Combining both bounds,
$$|X| = 2^{\aleph_0}.$$

This is the cardinality of the continuum $\mathfrak{c}$.
